notes: Dabhol CAR/DSU reinsurance premium dispute; Morison J's construction of Condition 12 and severability is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Swiss Re v UII: premium refund after abandonment of Dabhol Phase II project
key_facts: Swiss Re led a following market reinsurance of United India Insurance for the Dabhol Power Project Phase II construction and DSU cover.
Contractors abandoned the site in June 2001 after MSEB failed to pay under the power purchase agreement; work was largely complete but LNG testing remained outstanding.
Swiss Re continued cover under Condition 12 and Endorsement Dabhol until 17 December 2001, then treated the policy as lapsed.
UII claimed a refund of about US$8.5 million of premium; Swiss Re sought negative declaratory relief that no refund was due.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of Swiss Re's claim for declarations that the reinsurance had lawfully lapsed and UII's counterclaim for premium refund.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted for Swiss Re; counterclaim dismissed; no estoppel or implied term requiring refund; guarantee maintenance premium not severable.
enrichment.ratio: Condition 12 allowed cover to continue without additional premium for up to six months after a stoppage but did not extend the policy for the balance of the term absent further agreement; where work ceased the risk changed materially and the minimum premium was not apportionable between construction, testing and maintenance elements.
legal_issues: Construction of Condition 12 on cessation of works
Whether premium was apportionable after policy lapse
Whether guarantee maintenance cover had attached before abandonment
Whether estoppel by convention prevented denial of refund
linked_authorities: Re Drake Insurance Plc [2001] 1 Lloyd's Rep IR 643
Kausar v Eagle Star Insurance Co Ltd [2000] Lloyd's Rep IR 154

confidence.notes: Final declarations and detailed reasoning on premium, Condition 12 and estoppel are explicit.

notes: Long-running contact appeal; Wall LJ sets aside findings on domestic violence and PTSD and remits to Hedley J.

enrichment.short_title: Re F-K: contact appeal set aside after flawed re-hearing of domestic violence
key_facts: A ten-year-old girl's parents had a long history of contested contact proceedings following separation and alleged drug-fuelled violence by the father.
Judge Case had made findings of domestic violence and accepted a PTSD diagnosis for the mother; Judge Masterman later re-heard and rejected those findings.
Judge Masterman ordered regular Saturday contact collected by paternal grandparents; the mother appealed and contact was stayed pending appeal.
The mother contended that direct contact was insupportable given the father's violence and her PTSD.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal permission to appeal and appeal against a Children Act contact order after a late re-hearing before a different judge.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on five grounds; appeal allowed; contact order and violence/PTSD findings set aside; matter remitted to Hedley J for further directions and disposal.
enrichment.ratio: In intractable contact cases involving domestic violence the approach in Re L, V, M and H requires judicial continuity and careful treatment of accepted PTSD findings; a late re-examination of violence findings years after the event was an unsafe basis to overturn the established factual foundation of the case.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Masterman was plainly wrong to re-hear domestic violence allegations
Whether PTSD findings should have been overturned
Proper approach to contact where domestic violence is alleged
Whether pre-written judgment procedure breached Article 6
catchwords: Re L V M and H
linked_authorities: Re L, V, M and H (Contact: Domestic Violence) [2001] Fam 260

confidence.notes: Appellate order at paragraph 162 and remittal terms are clearly stated.

notes: Costs appeal in complex ancillary relief; Munby J applies FPR 2.69 after Norris on Calderbank offers and non-disclosure.

enrichment.short_title: H (S) v H: costs appeal after ancillary relief and misleading disclosure
key_facts: Following a nine-day ancillary relief hearing the wife was awarded about £237,500 but ordered to pay the husband's costs from November 2001.
The husband had made Calderbank offers of £200,000; the wife pursued a £275,000 sum said to have gone abroad and failed on major issues including stellar contribution.
The husband's solicitors gave misleading answers about the £275,000 having gone into his pension fund; the truth emerged only on appeal.
District Judge Brasse had relied on a flawed November 2001 will-based offer in making the costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a costs order made at the conclusion of contested ancillary relief proceedings, following an earlier successful appeal on quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; wife awarded 20% of costs of the nine-day hearing; 70% of appeal costs ordered against her; November offer-based costs order plainly wrong.
enrichment.ratio: Under FPR 2.69B/D and Norris, costs after Calderbank offers depend on all circumstances including disclosure; misleading information about a material asset can justify withholding costs from the paying party even where their final award exceeded offers, while unreasonable litigation conduct may still reduce recovery.
legal_issues: Application of FPR 2.69B to Calderbank offers in ancillary relief
Effect of non-disclosure of the £275,000 on costs
Whether November 2001 offer justified costs from that date
Cordle v Cordle test on appeal against costs discretion

confidence.notes: Final costs percentages and reasoning on offers and disclosure are clearly expressed.

notes: Short Eady J judgment continuing contra mundum injunction to protect Maxine Carr's identity.

enrichment.short_title: Carr v News Group: renewal of contra mundum injunction for new identity
key_facts: Maxine Carr sought a contra mundum injunction to protect her new identity and whereabouts after release.
Evidence showed continuing risk of serious physical and psychological harm if her location became public.
Similar injunctions had been effective since May 2004; probation, Home Office and police supported renewal.
Media defendants did not attend or contest the application but did not consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewal application for a confidential-information injunction of general effect binding anyone with notice.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction granted in the terms sought as necessary and proportionate to protect life and psychological integrity.
enrichment.ratio: The court must take reasonable measures under section 6 HRA to protect Articles 2 and 3; where objective evidence shows continuing danger, a contra mundum injunction restricting publication of identity and location may be necessary and proportionate even though legitimate public interest debates can proceed without those details.
legal_issues: Whether Articles 2 and 3 required protective injunction
Proportionality of restrictions on Article 10
Whether contra mundum scope was necessary
Legitimate public interest in rehabilitation costs and child protection lessons
linked_authorities: Venables and Thompson v News Group Newspapers [2001] Fam 430
X and Y v O'Brien [2003] EWHC 1101 (QB)

confidence.notes: Short judgment with clear outcome though detailed evidence is not reproduced for obvious reasons.

notes: Summary judgment on Jimi Hendrix Stockholm performer rights; Yameta management agreement defence rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Experience Hendrix v Purple Haze: summary judgment on Stockholm performer rights
key_facts: Experience Hendrix claimed infringement of Jimi Hendrix's performer rights in 1969 Stockholm concert recordings sold by Purple Haze Records.
Rights passed through Hendrix's estate to the claimant; Sweden became a qualifying country before the 1996 Regulations.
Defendants relied on the 1966 Yameta management agreement as assigning or licensing exploitation rights.
The first defendant sold unauthorised copies; the second defendant was alleged to be its controlling mind.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery summary judgment application under CPR 24.2 on performer rights infringement.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for the claimant against both defendants; Stockholm performances were qualifying performances and Yameta defences had no real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Performances in Sweden after it became a qualifying country are protected retrospectively; each performer in a group holds individual rights; a management agreement entitling the manager to commission on gross payments did not assign performer rights or authorise unlicensed copying.
legal_issues: Whether 1969 Stockholm performances were qualifying performances
Whether Hendrix alone or the band held the relevant rights
Effect of the Yameta Agreement on post-1989 and 1996 rights
Personal liability of the second defendant as joint tortfeasor
linked_authorities: MCA Records Inc v Charly Records [2002] EMLR 1
Rickless v United Artists Corp [1988] QB 40
CBS Songs Ltd v Amstrad Consumer Electronics plc [1988] AC 1013

confidence.notes: Summary judgment reasoning on qualifying performances and Yameta is detailed and conclusive.

notes: Article 6 reasonable time in section 16 DTA 1994 confiscation certificate proceedings; remittal to crown court.

enrichment.short_title: Re Saggar: Article 6 and delay in reopening drug confiscation realisable assets
key_facts: Sunil Saggar pleaded guilty in 1995 to drug import offences; a confiscation order was made for £1,370, the only realisable asset then identified.
Customs applied under section 16 in 2003 to certify increased realisable assets including a Bromley property worth about £735,000.
Saggar argued delay breached Article 6(1); Customs said section 16 proceedings were new and time ran only from 2003.
He had been told in 1999 that Customs had no intention of proceeding further at that time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a High Court preliminary issue granting a section 16 certificate after seven years' delay.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 16 certificate must issue; Article 6 reasonable time runs from the whole confiscation process but delay and remedy are for the crown court with abuse arguments.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 applies to section 16 reassessment of realisable assets and the reasonable time period covers the whole drug-trafficking proceedings, not only the certificate application; however whether delay is unreasonable and what remedy follows must be considered together with abuse of process at the section 16(4) stage rather than by refusing certification.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6 applies to section 16 proceedings
From when the reasonable time period runs
Whether seven years' delay was unreasonable
Whether breach required quashing the certificate
linked_authorities: R (Lloyd) v Bow Street Magistrates' Court [2004] 1 Cr App R 11

confidence.notes: Central Article 6 analysis and remittal approach are clearly reasoned though factual delay findings were not finally resolved.

notes: Landmark challenge to Bangladesh designation under section 94; inclusion on white list quashed but individual certification upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Husan: Bangladesh unlawfully designated under section 94 asylum white list
key_facts: Bangladesh was added to the section 94(4) designated states list in July 2003, triggering mandatory certification unless claims were not clearly unfounded.
The claimant, a Bangladeshi asylum seeker, challenged the lawfulness of Bangladesh's inclusion and the certification of his claim.
Objective country information documented widespread torture, political violence, violence against women and persecution of minorities.
The defendant relied on low asylum grant rates and constitutional protections; the court found the material drove only one rational conclusion against designation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of section 94 certification and of the Asylum (Designated States) (No.2) Order 2003 adding Bangladesh to the list.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that Bangladesh's inclusion in the list was unlawful; claim otherwise dismissed because the claimant's claim was clearly unfounded on internal relocation grounds.
enrichment.ratio: No rational decision-maker could have been satisfied under section 94(5) that there was in general no serious risk of persecution in Bangladesh or that removal would not generally breach Convention rights; terminological reverse in section 94(3) does not affect the section 94(2) clearly unfounded test applied to individual claims.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of adding Bangladesh to the section 94(4) list
Margin of appreciation in white list decisions
Whether section 94(3) tainted certification
Whether the claimant's claim was clearly unfounded

confidence.notes: Declaration on designation and separate certification analysis are both clearly reasoned.

notes: CPR 71 committal orders set aside for failure to comply with travelling expenses rules.

enrichment.short_title: Pelling v Bow County Court: committal orders set aside for CPR 71 breach
key_facts: Dr Pelling failed to attend examinations about his means in enforcement of a costs order from an unsuccessful judicial review challenge to court privacy rules.
Beatson J and Royce J made suspended committal orders after he failed to attend on 28 July and 26 October 2004.
The judgment creditor's affidavit did not state compliance with CPR 71.4 and 71.5 on travelling expenses.
Dr Pelling also sought Human Rights Act damages claims which the court adjourned generally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against suspended committal orders for failure to attend judgment debtor examinations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; both committal orders set aside; HRA damages claims adjourned generally with doubt expressed as to their prospects.
enrichment.ratio: A committal order for failing to attend court under CPR 71 may not be made unless the judgment creditor has complied with rules 71.4 and 71.5, including affidavit evidence about travelling expenses; non-compliance is fatal to validity.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 71.4 and 71.5 were complied with
Validity of suspended committal orders
Whether HRA claims could proceed in the Court of Appeal
Extension of time for appeal

confidence.notes: Conceded appeal on clear CPR 71 non-compliance; outcome and legal basis are straightforward.

notes: Reflective loss strike-out; corporate customer Pollux cannot be sidestepped by personal claim of shipowner.

enrichment.short_title: Diamantides v JP Morgan: strike out of shareholder's reflective loss claim
key_facts: Greek shipowner Mr Diamantides invested in Russian GKO-linked notes through Pollux, a Liberian company used as his investment vehicle.
Pollux had previously sued JP Morgan in New York; jurisdiction was rejected and Chase commenced English negative declaration proceedings.
Mr Diamantides then sued personally claiming he, not Pollux, was the bank's advisory customer entitled to private investor protection.
The bank applied to strike out the individual claim as a lawyers' construct with no loss distinct from Pollux's.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court strike-out application against the individual claimant's primary case in banking negligence and breach of duty.
enrichment.outcome: Individual claim struck out; no tenable case that Mr Diamantides alone was the customer; any loss would be reflective of Pollux's claim.
enrichment.ratio: Where investments were made through a wholly owned corporate vehicle that was the account holder and contracting party, a shareholder cannot pierce the corporate veil to sue as the personal customer; losses suffered through the company are reflective and recoverable only by the company under Johnson v Gore Wood principles.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Diamantides was the bank's customer in his personal capacity
Applicability of reflective loss in Johnson v Gore Wood
Whether advisory and transactional relationships could be split
Private investor status under section 62A FSA 1986
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Strike-out reasoning on customer relationship and reflective loss is explicit.

notes: Proprietary estoppel on Yeoman's Row development; lien for half planning uplift ordered, not constructive trust.

enrichment.short_title: Cobbe v Yeomans Row: lien for half planning permission uplift after joint venture
key_facts: Property developer James Cobbe agreed with Mrs Lisle-Mainwaring acting for Yeomans Row Management to seek planning permission to redevelop a Chelsea block of flats.
On success the property would be sold to Cobbe for £12m plus 50% overage above £24m gross proceeds; Cobbe spent time and money obtaining permission.
After permission was granted in March 2004 the defendants withdrew and sought to sell on improved terms without honouring the arrangement.
Cobbe claimed proprietary estoppel, constructive trust and restitution; the corporate owner was the proper defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of claims arising from an oral joint venture to obtain and exploit planning permission for redevelopment.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration of equitable lien for half the increase in property value attributable to planning permission as at 18 March 2004, conditional on sharing plans; claim against Mrs Lisle-Mainwaring dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: An equitable estoppel arose from Cobbe's reliance on a joint venture to obtain planning permission, but a lien for half the planning uplift was the appropriate remedy rather than a constructive trust; section 2 did not bar proprietary estoppel relief and the corporate veil could not be pierced against the directing mind personally.
legal_issues: Whether proprietary estoppel was established
Whether a constructive trust or lien was the appropriate remedy
Effect of section 2 on oral land agreements
Personal liability of Mrs Lisle-Mainwaring
linked_authorities: Banner Homes Group plc v Luff Developments Ltd [2000] Ch 372

confidence.notes: Final lien declaration and dismissal of personal claim are clearly stated though valuation remains to be determined.
